newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Allianz says on rising profit track.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Allianz says on rising profit track.

text.p: German insurance giant Allianz AG Holding on Wednesday said it was on track for further double-digit profit growth this year after its net earnings climbed some 10 percent in 1996.

Boosted last year by modest claims, foreign currency gains against the mark and booming capital markets, it said there was no reason for the earnings trend to break, despite only modest sales expansion in a sharply competitive market.
"The Allianz group's goal is to show a positive underwriting result in 1997," it said.
"Barring any major claims or natural catastrophes and assuming that capital markets will remain stable overall, Allianz projects that profits will show moderate double-digit growth this year."
Allianz said its 1996 pre-tax profit rose by a third to 4.1 billion marks ($2.4 billion), somewhat ahead of average forecasts, while net profits, as expected, rose more slowly to 2.2 billion.
The discrepancy between the rates of growth arose as Allianz could not use the one-off tax break which had inflated its 1995 net figure.
The group, which is now projecting earnings per share of 92 marks for 1996, up from 87.20 the previous year, plans to raise its 1996 dividend to 17 marks from 16.
The news had little impact on Allianz shares, which dropped 83 marks to 3,240 marks in bourse trade -- slightly weaker than an overall downward trend.

Analysts said the stock might be consolidating after weeks of rapid gains but the results should support longer-term interest in Allianz, which has benefited lately from a perceived increased emphasis on shareholder value.
"This is a conservative company and they are obviously in a good position to judge their own outlook," commented WestLB Research's head of financial research, Georg Kanders.
WestLB already has Allianz as a "strong buy" and plans to raise its earnings estimates for the stock for 1997 from the current 90 marks to at least 92 on the basis of the latest figures.
Allianz reported a six percent rise in its premium income to 74.7 billion marks and said that discounting special factors, sales would have risen only 4.8 percent.
Foreign currency gains inflated premiums by 2.1 billion marks.

However, changes such as Allianz's disposal mid-year of Deutsche Krankenversicherungs AG, as well as the consolidation of loan insurer Hermes and the Swiss Berner group, caused premiums to fall by 1.3 billion marks.

Underlying business, meanwhile, was uneven, with non-life premiums rising around nine percent despite a fall-off in business in the competitive newly deregulated markets of Germany, France and Switzerland and a mere 1.4 percent rise in life and health insurance premiums.

Allianz conceded that the environment for insurance was tough, saying: "Competition will be consistently tough on the most important markets. Therefore the further streamlining of operations and efforts to cut costs will assume greater importance as competitive factors."

The insurer aims to turn an underwriting profit in 1997 after careful risk selection and modest claims helped it narrow its stubbornly persistent underwriting loss by some 500 million marks to 150 million in 1996.
In 1996, non-underwriting earnings rose 14 percent to 4.3 billion amid positive developments on capital markets.

The current year also promises growth in sales -- this year's consolidation of the Vereinte insurance group, which it took over in a complex share swap with Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG, should lift premiums by 12 percent to some 84 billion marks. ($ = 1.693 German Marks)
